content.text: I have everything I need. Writing up the comparison now.

answers.answer:
## What changed

In SCOP 1.75 (frozen 2009-02-23), PDB 1acc chain A, the anthrax protective antigen, was a single whole-chain domain:

- d1acca_, sunid 43828, sccs f.11.1.1, region "1acc A:" (no residue range, i.e. the entire chain)
- Lineage: class f (membrane and cell surface proteins and peptides) -> fold f.11 "Anthrax protective antigen" (sunid 56987) -> superfamily f.11.1 (sunid 56988) -> family f.11.1.1 (sunid 56989) -> protein "Anthrax protective antigen" (sunid 56990) -> species Bacillus anthracis TaxId 1392 (sunid 56991)
- That superfamily held exactly one family, which in turn held one protein and one species. It was a singleton branch built around this one structure.

The definition survived the three SCOPe releases that were relabelled 1.75A, 1.75B and 1.75C. I queried 1acc in 2.01, 2.02 and 2.03 and got the identical single d1acca_ record with the same sunid each time.

The split appears in SCOPe 2.04 (freeze 2014-04-15, public 2014-07-11) and is unchanged in the current release 2.08 (public 2021-09-22, latest periodic update 2.08-2026-08-16). Chain A now carries two domains:

| New domain | sunid | Region | sccs |
|---|---|---|---|
| d1acca2 | 238522 | 1acc A:14-225 | b.179.1.1 |
| d1acca1 | 238521 | 1acc A:226-735 | f.60.1.1 |

The old identifiers are retired, not aliased. Requesting sunid 43828 or sid d1acca_ in release 2.08 returns 404, and the old fold f.11 is absent from 2.08 as well.

The two halves did not stay together.

- The C-terminal part kept the membrane class but moved to a renamed branch: class f -> fold f.60 "Anthrax protective antigen C-terminal-like" (sunid 254103) -> superfamily f.60.1 (254122) -> family f.60.1.1 (254146) -> protein (254333) -> species B. anthracis TaxId 1392 (254762). This branch is still a singleton: one family under the superfamily.
- The N-terminal part crossed a class boundary. It is now class b (all beta proteins) -> fold b.179 "Anthrax protective antigen N-terminal-like" (254104) -> superfamily b.179.1 "PA14-like" (254123) -> family b.179.1.1 "PA14" (254147) -> protein "PA14" (254334) -> species Bacillus anthracis (254763). Neither b.179 nor any PA14-like node existed in 1.75.

So this is not a boundary tweak. One SCOP leaf became two leaves in two different classes, and a brand-new superfamily was created to hold the smaller one.

## Why the N-terminal module is the interesting half

The new PA14-like superfamily is populated, unlike the branch it came from. It holds four families: b.179.1.1 PA14, b.179.1.2 GLEYA domain, b.179.1.3 glycoside hydrolase family 31 (GH31) PA14-like domain, and b.179.1.0 automated matches.

The company this module keeps is the point. Inside the single family b.179.1.1 there are two proteins: "PA14" from Bacillus anthracis, and "Beta-glucosidase PA14 domain" from Kluyveromyces marxianus, represented by d3abza3 at 3abz A:388-559 and seven sibling domains from 3abz and 3ac0. The sister families are a Saccharomyces cerevisiae adhesin GLEYA domain (d2xjpa1 at 2xjp A:23-271 and relatives) and an alpha-xylosidase. A bacterial toxin subunit, a yeast beta-glucosidase, a fungal cell-wall adhesin and a glycosidase all share one superfamily, and the first two share a family.

Note the residue ranges. In anthrax PA the module sits at the N-terminus, residues 14-225. In the yeast beta-glucosidase it is an internal insertion, residues 388-559 of a longer chain, flanked by catalytic machinery on both sides. The same evolutionary unit occupies a different position in a different host protein.

That is what makes a domain an evolutionary module rather than a convenient piece of a picture. The unit that recombines, that gets inserted into an unrelated catalytic scaffold and carries a ligand-binding beta-sandwich with it, is the 212-residue PA14 region, not chain A. SCOP 1.75 drew the boundary at the chain and thereby named a one-member fold after a single toxin. SCOPe 2.04 redrew it at the recombination unit, and the moment it did, relatives appeared across three kingdoms. The 1.75 classification was not wrong about the structure; it was wrong about the unit of descent.

## The same recut applied across the PA entries

This was a systematic recut, not a one-off. In 2.08, 1t6b chain X splits as d1t6bx1 (X:226-735, f.60.1.1) and d1t6bx2 (X:16-225, b.179.1.1), alongside the receptor domain d1t6by_ (c.62.1.1). 3tew chain A splits at the same seam, A:226-735 and A:15-225.

The PA63 structures expose a biological subtlety. In the heptameric prepore 1tzo, every chain gives an f.60.1.1 domain at 226-735, but the b.179.1.1 domain is only A:174-225 and the equivalent in chains B through O, and 3j9c A:174-225 behaves the same way. Furin cleavage removes domain 1a, so in those entries only a 52-residue remnant of the PA14 module is present. The module is physically excised during activation. Across the B. anthracis species node under the PA14 family, the boundaries run 14-225, 15-225, 16-225 and 174-225 depending on the entry.

## How this should change homology searching

**Search per-domain, against a current release.** A full-chain profile built from 1acc buries a 212-residue module inside 735 residues. The PA14 signal is diluted and a genuine remote hit to a glycosidase can fall below threshold. Legacy resources still carry the old answer: anything keyed to SCOP 1.75 or ASTRAL 1.75 sets, including trained classifiers and published benchmarks, reports f.11.1.1 for this chain and has no PA14 superfamily at all. Benchmarks built on 1.75 will score a correct modern PA14 assignment as an error.

**Remap identifiers rather than assuming continuity.** sunid 43828 is dead and d1acca_ no longer resolves. A pipeline that caches SCOP identifiers must re-resolve against the current release through the PDB-to-domains route rather than trusting a stored sid.

**Do not transfer function across the seam.** A query that matches d1acca2 has acquired evidence for a PA14-like beta-sandwich module, which in this family is associated with carbohydrate and ligand binding. It has acquired no evidence that the query is a toxin, forms a pore, oligomerises into a heptamer, or binds the anthrax toxin receptor. Those properties belong to d1acca1 and to the quaternary assembly. The reverse transfer is equally unsafe: a hit to d1acca1 says nothing about whether the query carries a PA14 module. Under the 1.75 single-domain record, both of these errors were easy to make, because any hit anywhere in the chain inherited the label "anthrax protective antigen".

**Calibrate the inference to the level.** Family b.179.1.1 is where the caution bites hardest here, because that family already spans a toxin subunit and a yeast beta-glucosidase accessory domain. Even a family-level assignment does not transfer enzymatic activity or toxicity; it transfers module identity and, at best, a general ligand-binding role. Superfamily b.179.1 asserts common ancestry with divergent function. Fold-level similarity between b.179 and anything else, or between f.60 and anything else, asserts no homology at all. And f.60.1 remains a one-family singleton, so a hit there buys you no comparative evidence from relatives.

**Check the representative before using it as a template.** ASTRAL and other non-redundant sets pick one domain per cluster. If the chosen b.179.1.1 representative comes from a PA63 entry such as 1tzo or 3j9c, you get a 52-residue fragment at 174-225, a partial module that will align badly and model worse. Always inspect the residue range of the representative you were handed, not just its sccs. For modelling, use d1acca2 and d1acca1 as separate templates with their own boundaries; threading a PA14-only query onto the full 1acc chain produces a spurious alignment over 510 unrelated residues.

**A caveat on the C-terminal domain.** SCOPe keeps 226-735 as one unit, while the structural literature on PA describes it as several domains, including the beta-barrel pore-forming region and the C-terminal receptor-binding domain. The 2.04 recut fixed the evolutionarily important seam; it did not decompose the remainder. Treat f.60.1.1 as a composite for template and function-transfer purposes.

## Limits and external evidence needed

I verified the single-domain state in 1.75, 2.01, 2.02 and 2.03 and the split state in 2.04 and 2.08. I did not query 2.05, 2.06 or 2.07; since 2.04 and 2.08 carry identical sunids and boundaries, the definition is stable across that span, but I am stating that as inference rather than direct observation.

The SCOPe records give classification, not the reasoning behind it. Confirming the PA14 homology argument on its own terms needs profile-profile or HMM comparison such as HHpred, structural superposition such as DALI between d1acca2 and d3abza3, the corresponding Pfam PA14 entry, and the primary literature that identified PA14 as a mobile module across glycosidases, glycosyltransferases, adhesins and toxins. The furin-cleavage interpretation of the 174-225 fragments comes from anthrax toxin biochemistry, not from SCOPe. Structure quality for 1acc is X-ray at 2.1 angstrom with R-factor 0.223 and SPACI 0.370, adequate for domain assignment and templating.

One caution on the taxonomy itself. The two species nodes are annotated inconsistently: the f.60.1.1 node reads "Anthrax bacillus (Bacillus anthracis) [TaxId: 1392]" while the b.179.1.1 node reads simply "Bacillus anthracis" with no TaxId. Do not rely on SCOPe species strings for taxonomic filtering; resolve organisms against the PDB or NCBI taxonomy instead.
evidence_used: pretrained model knowledge of anthrax protective antigen architecture, furin activation of PA83 to PA63, and the PA14 module as a mobile carbohydrate-binding element in glycosidases and adhesins

- d1acca_, sunid 43828, sccs f.11.1.1, region "1acc A:" (no residue range, i.e. the entire chain)
- Lineage: class f (membrane and cell surface proteins and peptides) -> fold f.11 "Anthrax protective antigen" (sunid 56987) -> superfamily f.11.1 (sunid 56988) -> family f.11.1.1 (sunid 56989) -> protein "Anthrax protective antigen" (sunid 56990) -> species Bacillus anthracis TaxId 1392 (sunid 56991)
- That superfamily held exactly one family, which in turn held one protein and one species. It was a singleton branch built around this one structure.

The definition survived the three SCOPe releases that were relabelled 1.75A, 1.75B and 1.75C. I queried 1acc in 2.01, 2.02 and 2.03 and got the identical single d1acca_ record with the same sunid each time.

The split appears in SCOPe 2.04 (freeze 2014-04-15, public 2014-07-11) and is unchanged in the current release 2.08 (public 2021-09-22, latest periodic update 2.08-2026-08-16). Chain A now carries two domains:

| New domain | sunid | Region | sccs |
|---|---|---|---|
| d1acca2 | 238522 | 1acc A:14-225 | b.179.1.1 |
| d1acca1 | 238521 | 1acc A:226-735 | f.60.1.1 |

The old identifiers are retired, not aliased. Requesting sunid 43828 or sid d1acca_ in release 2.08 returns 404, and the old fold f.11 is absent from 2.08 as well.

The two halves did not stay together.

- The C-terminal part kept the membrane class but moved to a renamed branch: class f -> fold f.60 "Anthrax protective antigen C-terminal-like" (sunid 254103) -> superfamily f.60.1 (254122) -> family f.60.1.1 (254146) -> protein (254333) -> species B. anthracis TaxId 1392 (254762). This branch is still a singleton: one family under the superfamily.
- The N-terminal part crossed a class boundary. It is now class b (all beta proteins) -> fold b.179 "Anthrax protective antigen N-terminal-like" (254104) -> superfamily b.179.1 "PA14-like" (254123) -> family b.179.1.1 "PA14" (254147) -> protein "PA14" (254334) -> species Bacillus anthracis (254763). Neither b.179 nor any PA14-like node existed in 1.75.

So this is not a boundary tweak. One SCOP leaf became two leaves in two different classes, and a brand-new superfamily was created to hold the smaller one.

## Why the N-terminal module is the interesting half

The new PA14-like superfamily is populated, unlike the branch it came from. It holds four families: b.179.1.1 PA14, b.179.1.2 GLEYA domain, b.179.1.3 glycoside hydrolase family 31 (GH31) PA14-like domain, and b.179.1.0 automated matches.

The company this module keeps is the point. Inside the single family b.179.1.1 there are two proteins: "PA14" from Bacillus anthracis, and "Beta-glucosidase PA14 domain" from Kluyveromyces marxianus, represented by d3abza3 at 3abz A:388-559 and seven sibling domains from 3abz and 3ac0. The sister families are a Saccharomyces cerevisiae adhesin GLEYA domain (d2xjpa1 at 2xjp A:23-271 and relatives) and an alpha-xylosidase. A bacterial toxin subunit, a yeast beta-glucosidase, a fungal cell-wall adhesin and a glycosidase all share one superfamily, and the first two share a family.

Note the residue ranges. In anthrax PA the module sits at the N-terminus, residues 14-225. In the yeast beta-glucosidase it is an internal insertion, residues 388-559 of a longer chain, flanked by catalytic machinery on both sides. The same evolutionary unit occupies a different position in a different host protein.

That is what makes a domain an evolutionary module rather than a convenient piece of a picture. The unit that recombines, that gets inserted into an unrelated catalytic scaffold and carries a ligand-binding beta-sandwich with it, is the 212-residue PA14 region, not chain A. SCOP 1.75 drew the boundary at the chain and thereby named a one-member fold after a single toxin. SCOPe 2.04 redrew it at the recombination unit, and the moment it did, relatives appeared across three kingdoms. The 1.75 classification was not wrong about the structure; it was wrong about the unit of descent.

## The same recut applied across the PA entries

This was a systematic recut, not a one-off. In 2.08, 1t6b chain X splits as d1t6bx1 (X:226-735, f.60.1.1) and d1t6bx2 (X:16-225, b.179.1.1), alongside the receptor domain d1t6by_ (c.62.1.1). 3tew chain A splits at the same seam, A:226-735 and A:15-225.

The PA63 structures expose a biological subtlety. In the heptameric prepore 1tzo, every chain gives an f.60.1.1 domain at 226-735, but the b.179.1.1 domain is only A:174-225 and the equivalent in chains B through O, and 3j9c A:174-225 behaves the same way. Furin cleavage removes domain 1a, so in those entries only a 52-residue remnant of the PA14 module is present. The module is physically excised during activation. Across the B. anthracis species node under the PA14 family, the boundaries run 14-225, 15-225, 16-225 and 174-225 depending on the entry.

## How this should change homology searching

**Search per-domain, against a current release.** A full-chain profile built from 1acc buries a 212-residue module inside 735 residues. The PA14 signal is diluted and a genuine remote hit to a glycosidase can fall below threshold. Legacy resources still carry the old answer: anything keyed to SCOP 1.75 or ASTRAL 1.75 sets, including trained classifiers and published benchmarks, reports f.11.1.1 for this chain and has no PA14 superfamily at all. Benchmarks built on 1.75 will score a correct modern PA14 assignment as an error.

**Remap identifiers rather than assuming continuity.** sunid 43828 is dead and d1acca_ no longer resolves. A pipeline that caches SCOP identifiers must re-resolve against the current release through the PDB-to-domains route rather than trusting a stored sid.

**Do not transfer function across the seam.** A query that matches d1acca2 has acquired evidence for a PA14-like beta-sandwich module, which in this family is associated with carbohydrate and ligand binding. It has acquired no evidence that the query is a toxin, forms a pore, oligomerises into a heptamer, or binds the anthrax toxin receptor. Those properties belong to d1acca1 and to the quaternary assembly. The reverse transfer is equally unsafe: a hit to d1acca1 says nothing about whether the query carries a PA14 module. Under the 1.75 single-domain record, both of these errors were easy to make, because any hit anywhere in the chain inherited the label "anthrax protective antigen".

**Calibrate the inference to the level.** Family b.179.1.1 is where the caution bites hardest here, because that family already spans a toxin subunit and a yeast beta-glucosidase accessory domain. Even a family-level assignment does not transfer enzymatic activity or toxicity; it transfers module identity and, at best, a general ligand-binding role. Superfamily b.179.1 asserts common ancestry with divergent function. Fold-level similarity between b.179 and anything else, or between f.60 and anything else, asserts no homology at all. And f.60.1 remains a one-family singleton, so a hit there buys you no comparative evidence from relatives.

**Check the representative before using it as a template.** ASTRAL and other non-redundant sets pick one domain per cluster. If the chosen b.179.1.1 representative comes from a PA63 entry such as 1tzo or 3j9c, you get a 52-residue fragment at 174-225, a partial module that will align badly and model worse. Always inspect the residue range of the representative you were handed, not just its sccs. For modelling, use d1acca2 and d1acca1 as separate templates with their own boundaries; threading a PA14-only query onto the full 1acc chain produces a spurious alignment over 510 unrelated residues.

**A caveat on the C-terminal domain.** SCOPe keeps 226-735 as one unit, while the structural literature on PA describes it as several domains, including the beta-barrel pore-forming region and the C-terminal receptor-binding domain. The 2.04 recut fixed the evolutionarily important seam; it did not decompose the remainder. Treat f.60.1.1 as a composite for template and function-transfer purposes.

## Limits and external evidence needed

I verified the single-domain state in 1.75, 2.01, 2.02 and 2.03 and the split state in 2.04 and 2.08. I did not query 2.05, 2.06 or 2.07; since 2.04 and 2.08 carry identical sunids and boundaries, the definition is stable across that span, but I am stating that as inference rather than direct observation.

The SCOPe records give classification, not the reasoning behind it. Confirming the PA14 homology argument on its own terms needs profile-profile or HMM comparison such as HHpred, structural superposition such as DALI between d1acca2 and d3abza3, the corresponding Pfam PA14 entry, and the primary literature that identified PA14 as a mobile module across glycosidases, glycosyltransferases, adhesins and toxins. The furin-cleavage interpretation of the 174-225 fragments comes from anthrax toxin biochemistry, not from SCOPe. Structure quality for 1acc is X-ray at 2.1 angstrom with R-factor 0.223 and SPACI 0.370, adequate for domain assignment and templating.

One caution on the taxonomy itself. The two species nodes are annotated inconsistently: the f.60.1.1 node reads "Anthrax bacillus (Bacillus anthracis) [TaxId: 1392]" while the b.179.1.1 node reads simply "Bacillus anthracis" with no TaxId.
